misconception_description: Student believes that values must be explicitly converted to their current type to ensure type safety.

solutions.generated_code:
program PalindromBerikutnya
kamus
  n, kandidat, sisa, hasilBalik : integer
  sudahKetemu : boolean
algoritma
  input(n)
  kandidat <- integer(n) + 1
  sudahKetemu <- boolean(false)
  while not sudahKetemu do
    sisa <- integer(kandidat)
    hasilBalik <- integer(0)
    while integer(sisa) > 0 do
      hasilBalik <- integer(hasilBalik) * 10 + (integer(sisa) mod 10)
      sisa <- integer(sisa) div 10
    endwhile
    if integer(hasilBalik) == integer(kandidat) then
      sudahKetemu <- boolean(true)
    else
      kandidat <- integer(kandidat) + 1
    endif
  endwhile
  output(integer(kandidat))
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student adds unnecessary explicit type conversions throughout the code: converting num to int with int(num) even though it's already an integer parameter, converting i to int with int(i) even though range() yields integers, and converting the return value to int even though i is already an integer. The student genuinely believes these conversions are necessary for type safety and proper program behavior, similar to how some statically-typed languages require explicit type declarations. The code still functions correctly despite the redundant operations.
